metaDesc: Wat Lan Khuat (Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew) in Khun Han, Sisaket, Thailand is built from over 1.5 million glass bottles, with a temple on the water as its highlight. Travel guide, hours, photo spots, and nearby places to visit.
keywords: Wat Lan Khuat, Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew, temple of a million bottles, Khun Han, Sisaket, things to do in Sisaket, temple on the water
h1:
Wat Lan Khuat, Sisaket
The Temple Built From a Million Glass Bottles
intro: Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew, better known to most people as Wat Lan Khuat (the Temple of a Million Bottles), sits in Khun Han district, Sisaket. It's a temple decorated head to toe with more than 1.5 million recycled glass bottles, from the entrance arches to the ordination hall, the pavilions, and even the bathrooms. When the sun hits, all those bottles light up in a wash of colors, and the result is unlike any other temple in Thailand.

blocks.html: If you're road-tripping through Sisaket and want a stop you'll still remember years later, Wat Lan Khuat is about as memorable as it gets. The official name is Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew, in Ban Don, Non Sung subdistrict, Khun Han district. What sets it apart is that everything in the temple is decorated with recycled glass bottles — beer bottles, liquor bottles, soda bottles — roughly 1.5 million of them in total, arranged into patterns across the walls, columns, arches, and roofs.

What makes this place interesting beyond the novelty is the story behind it. Construction began around 1984 on the initiative of Phra Khru Wiwek Thammachan, or Luang Pu Lot, who came to practice meditation in the area and saw discarded bottles littered everywhere as garbage. He started collecting bottles from the surrounding villages to build the first monk's quarters, then slowly expanded until the whole temple took shape. The idea was for the clear bottles to serve as a dhamma riddle — when struck by sunlight, they shine like the light of the teachings.
Wat Lan Khuat is more than just walls of bottles — each spot is laid out so you can walk a full loop and take it all in. These are the parts people talk about most after a visit.

items.name: Temple on the water
items.blurb: Also called the sim klang nam, this four-gabled ordination hall stands right in the middle of a pond and is the most photographed spot in the temple. Inside sits a white jade Buddha image, and the reflection on the water looks best in the morning and late afternoon.

items.name: The great glass chedi
items.blurb: A large stupa covered in glass bottles from top to bottom — the source of the temple's official name. From a distance you can see the bottles shimmering in tiers.

items.name: Pavilions and entrance arches
items.blurb: From the entrance and the gateway arches to the bell tower and the monks' quarters, everything is laid out in bottle patterns. It's easy to lose track of time studying the details up close.

blocks.title: Best times for photos
blocks.html: Morning sun before 10 a.m. and the late afternoon before 5 p.m. are when the bottles catch the light best. Midday sun is harsh and very hot, and shooting into the glare is tricky. Come early or late and you'll have a far more comfortable time.

items: Opening hours — open daily, roughly 8 a.m.–5 p.m. (sometimes from early morning, since it's a working temple where monks actually live)
Admission — free; it's a temple, so entry is free, though there's a donation box if you'd like to contribute toward its upkeep
Dress code — dress modestly, as this is temple grounds with resident monks; avoid very short shorts or spaghetti straps
Time needed — about 45 minutes to an hour covers the whole place; allow around 1.5 hours if you're serious about photos

blocks.html: The temple is in Khun Han district, about 60 km from Sisaket town, roughly an hour and a bit by car. The main route follows Highway 211 onto 2111, passing through Phayu and Phrai Bueng districts on the way to Khun Han. The roads are good and the signage is clear; just drop "Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew" into your map and it'll take you straight there.

items: Self-drive — by far the easiest option, with a large parking lot. Khun Han's attractions are spread out, so having your own vehicle makes it much simpler to keep exploring afterward.
No car? — public transport is hard to come by here. Renting a car in Sisaket town or hiring a local driver for a round trip is the way to go.
From Ubon — coming from Ubon Ratchathani, you can drive via Det Udom and on to Khun Han; the distance is similar to coming from Sisaket town.

blocks.text: Where to go next around Khun Han

blocks.html: Khun Han borders the Phanom Dong Rak mountain range and has waterfalls, durian orchards, and Khmer ruins. If you've driven all the way out here, it's worth lining up a few more stops to make the trip count.

items.name: Huai Chan Waterfall
items.blurb: A waterfall in the Khun Han forest, good for a swim toward the end of the rainy season, with shady, relaxed surroundings. It's a short drive from the temple and makes a nice afternoon stop.

items.name: Volcanic-soil durian orchards
items.blurb: Sisaket is famous for durian grown in volcanic soil. Khun Han and Kantharalak have orchards where you can stop to taste it, roughly in season from June through August.

items.name: Khmer ruins in the province
items.blurb: Sisaket has several Khmer-era ruins, such as Prasat Sa Kamphaeng Yai and Prasat Ban Prasat, ideal if you want to add a culture-focused leg to the trip.

blocks.title: If you're heading to the Pha Mo I Daeng–Preah Vihear side
blocks.html: The attractions on the Kantharalak side, like Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan National Park, sit right on the Thailand–Cambodia border. At times the border situation leads to closures or restricted access. Before planning a trip to that area, always check the latest situation with the park or the province's official page first.

items: Less crowded than big-city temples — weekdays are quiet and easy, with no jostling for angles. Long weekends get busier but never packed.
Genuinely hot at midday — it's a forest temple with open areas and strong sun, so bring a hat and water. Mornings and evenings are far more comfortable.
Still an active place of practice — it's not just a photo stop; monks live here, so keep your voice down and be respectful of the place.
Worth the drive — it's a fair distance from town, but pairing it with other stops around Khun Han makes the trip far more worthwhile than coming for the one temple and turning back.

faq.q: Where is Wat Lan Khuat and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's in Ban Don, Non Sung subdistrict, Khun Han district, Sisaket province, about 60 km from Sisaket town — roughly an hour and a bit by car. Take Highway 211 onto 2111 through Phayu and Phrai Bueng. Self-driving or renting a car is recommended, as public transport is hard to come by.

faq.q: What are Wat Lan Khuat's hours, and is there an admission fee?
faq.a: It's open daily, roughly 8 a.m.–5 p.m., and entry is free with no admission charge. There's only a donation box if you'd like to contribute toward the temple's upkeep.

faq.q: Why is it called the Temple of a Million Bottles?
faq.a: Because the entire temple is decorated with around 1.5 million recycled glass bottles. It began when Luang Pu Lot collected discarded bottles that had been left as garbage and used them to build, intending the clear, light-reflecting bottles to act as a dhamma riddle for visitors. Its official name is Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew.

faq.q: What's the best photo spot at Wat Lan Khuat?
faq.a: The highlight is the temple on the water (sim klang nam), a four-gabled hall standing in the middle of a pond. It looks best in the morning before 10 a.m. and in the late afternoon before 5 p.m., when the sun makes the bottles shine and the pond water is still.

faq.q: What can you pair with a visit to Wat Lan Khuat?
faq.a: Khun Han has Huai Chan Waterfall and seasonal volcanic-soil durian orchards, and the province has several Khmer ruins. If you want to head over to Pha Mo I Daeng or Preah Vihear near the border, check the latest situation before you go.
